topic: Azure AI / Foundry: model deployment security, content filters, data grounding, prompt injection, data exfiltration, network isolation for AI

source_pages.title: Configure AI Gateway in your Foundry resources

questions.explanation: Correct: the content filtering system runs both prompt and completion through classification models, covers hate, sexual, violence and self-harm across safe, low, medium and high, and the default is medium severity for both prompts and completions. A is wrong: prompts are also filtered. C is wrong: the categories are hate, sexual, violence and self-harm; there is no financial-advice harm category. D is wrong: there is a configurable default, medium.
options: It has no default configuration, filtering is off until a filter is created
It filters only the models output; prompts are never filtered
It runs both prompt and completion through classification models for hate, sexual, violence and self-harm, defaulting to medium severity for both
It filters only financial advice and legal advice categories
questions.question: A team deploys a model in Microsoft Foundry with the default content filter. A user submits a prompt containing hate content and the model returns a violent completion. Which statement correctly describes what the default filter checks?
questions.source_quote: The default content filtering configuration is set to filter at the medium severity threshold for all four content harms categories for both prompts and completions.

questions.explanation: Correct: direct attacks are user prompts designed to jailbreak the model; indirect (cross-domain) attacks are malicious instructions hidden in documents the AI can access and process. A is wrong: that reverses the two. C is wrong: the distinction is about where the instruction comes from, not network versus billing. D is wrong: Prompt Shields covers both direct and indirect attacks.
options: Direct attacks target the network; indirect attacks target the billing system
Prompt Shields only detects direct attacks; indirect attacks cannot be detected
Direct attacks hide instructions in documents; indirect attacks are typed by the user
Direct attacks are user prompts designed to jailbreak the model; indirect attacks are malicious instructions placed in documents or data the AI reads
questions.question: An agent reads a supplier PDF that contains hidden instructions telling it to email internal pricing to an external address. The user never typed those instructions. Which attack is this, and how does it differ from a direct attack?
questions.source_quote: Prompt Shields for indirect attacks: Filter / annotate Indirect Attacks, also referred to as Indirect Prompt Attacks or Cross-Domain Prompt Injection Attacks, a potential vulnerability where third parties place malicious instructions inside of documents that the generative AI system can access and process.

questions.explanation: Correct: standard call-count limiting does not prevent cost overruns because one request can consume thousands of tokens; the token-limit policy governs by token usage (tokens-per-minute). A is wrong: call-count limits alone leave token burn ungoverned. C is wrong: the gateway is the enforcement point in front of the model, not a billing dashboard. D is wrong: token limits apply per project regardless of which application or agent calls.
options: Setting a daily call quota only, because token usage is fixed per call
Limiting calls per minute is enough, because every call costs the same
Token-based rate limiting (tokens-per-minute), because a single request can consume thousands of tokens and call-count limits do not cap token burn
Removing the gateway and letting apps call the model directly with their own API keys
questions.question: Three applications share one Foundry model deployment. One app sends a few very long prompts and exhausts the provisioned throughput, starving the others, even though it stays under a 100-calls-per-minute limit. Which AI Gateway control fixes this?
questions.source_quote: Limits apply at the project level. That is, each project can have its own TPM and quota settings. TPM rate limit: Limits token consumption to a configured maximum per minute.

questions.explanation: Correct: Defender for AI Services is the Defender for Cloud plan toggled on for the subscription (Environment settings, Defender plans, AI services) that protects Foundry workloads and gives real-time threat insights. A is wrong: a firewall alone does not give runtime AI threat detection. C is wrong: DSPM for AI is a Purview data-security capability, not the Defender plan. D is wrong: disabling content filters does not help Defender see prompts; it removes a guardrail.
options: Enable Purview DSPM for AI and stop, because that is the same plan as Defender for AI Services
Disable content filters so Defender can see the raw prompts more easily
Enable Azure Firewall on the virtual network only
Enable the Defender for AI Services plan in Defender for Cloud (Environment settings, Defender plans) for the subscription hosting the Foundry workloads
questions.question: A company runs generative AI applications in Microsoft Foundry and wants real-time threat protection and alerts for those workloads in Defender for Cloud. What is the first step, and which lookalike control is not the same plan?
questions.source_quote: Microsoft Defender for Cloud AI threat protection provides runtime detection of AI-specific attacks such as direct and indirect prompt injection and data exfiltration attempts, with alerts correlated in Defender XDR.

questions.explanation: Correct: the default is medium for all four harm categories for prompts and completions; all customers can modify thresholds, but turning filters partially or fully off requires approval (modified content filtering), and protected-material models may be required for Customer Copyright Commitment coverage; also the filtering system does not apply to audio models such as Whisper. A is wrong: turning filters off needs approval and is not a free toggle. C is wrong: the default is medium, not high. D is wrong: filtering applies to text and image models; Whisper audio models are the exclusion.
options: Disable filtering only for Whisper and keep it for text models, because Whisper is the only model the filter applies to
Turn the content filter off for the deployment in the portal; any customer can disable filtering without approval

Keep the default medium threshold for prompts and completions, apply for approval if filtering must be reduced, and keep protected-material models on where copyright coverage is required; note the filter does not apply to Whisper audio models
Set all categories to high and assume that is the default; the default is high for prompts and off for completions
questions.question: A team wants to turn off content filtering for a Foundry deployment to reduce false positives, and assumes the default is high severity. Which statement correctly describes the default, the off-switch, and the scope?
questions.source_quote: All customers have the ability to modify the content filters and configure the severity thresholds (low, medium, high). Approval is required for turning the content filters partially or fully off.

questions.explanation: Correct: the filter table states Prompt Shields for direct attacks (jailbreak) is on by default, while Prompt Shields for indirect attacks is off by default and must be enabled to catch instructions hidden in documents the agent reads. A is wrong: it reverses the defaults. C is wrong: indirect attacks are a distinct, detectable category (cross-domain prompt injection). D is wrong: direct and indirect are different detections; enabling one does not enable the other.
options: Prompt Shields covers only direct attacks; indirect attacks are not a recognised category
Enabling direct Prompt Shields automatically enables indirect Prompt Shields with the same setting
Direct Prompt Shields is off by default and indirect is on by default, so the agent is already protected against document attacks
Direct Prompt Shields (jailbreak) is on by default; indirect Prompt Shields is off by default and must be enabled to catch instructions hidden in documents the agent reads
questions.question: An agent reads customer documents and follows hidden instructions inside them. The team checks the Foundry content filter and finds Prompt Shields is on. Why is the agent still vulnerable to this document attack?
questions.source_quote: Prompt Shields for direct attacks (jailbreak): GA, On. Prompt Shields for indirect attacks: GA, Off. Filter / annotate Indirect Attacks, also referred to as Cross-Domain Prompt Injection Attacks.

questions.explanation: Correct: TPM rate-limit excess returns 429 Too Many Requests and total quota excess returns 403 Forbidden, limits apply per project, and call-count limiting is insufficient because one call can burn thousands of tokens. A is wrong: it inverts the status codes. C is wrong: the token-limit policy rejects before the backend is called, so it prevents token burn, not just reports it. D is wrong: limits apply at project level, so one projects burn does not automatically cap another.
options: Limits apply at the tenant level, so one projects overuse automatically blocks every other project
Exceeding the TPM limit returns 403 and exceeding the total quota returns 429; limits apply at the subscription level for all projects
Exceeding the TPM rate limit returns 429 Too Many Requests and exceeding the total token quota returns 403 Forbidden; limits are set per project, and call-count limits alone do not stop token burn
Token limits are a billing report only; a request that exceeds the limit still reaches the model and consumes tokens
questions.question: Two Foundry projects share an AI Gateway. Project A exceeds its tokens-per-minute limit; Project B exceeds its monthly total token quota. Which HTTP responses do the callers get, and at what scope are the limits set?
questions.source_quote: TPM rate limit: When requests exceed the TPM limit, the caller receives a 429 Too Many Requests response status code. Total token quota: When requests exceed the quota, the caller receives a 403 Forbidden response status code. Limits apply at the project level.

questions.explanation: Correct: data security for AI interactions (Purview access to prompts and responses, classification, auditing, eDiscovery) requires a Purview licence and is NOT included in the Defender for AI Services plan; with user prompt evidence disabled, Defender still analyses prompts and responses but masks the content in alerts; and Purview integration does not include data or context from Foundry agents at the time of the doc. A is wrong: the Purview licence is separate. C is wrong: disabling prompt evidence masks content in alerts, it does not stop detection. D is wrong: Defender alone does not provide eDiscovery or insider-risk review.
options: Disable user prompt evidence to stop Defender analysing prompts entirely
Rely on Defender for AI Services alone for eDiscovery and insider-risk review of AI interactions
Enabling Defender for AI Services automatically includes the Purview licence and full Foundry agent context

Enable Defender for AI Services, then separately licence and enable Purview data security for AI interactions; keep user prompt evidence on if triage needs the suspicious prompt segments (detection continues with masked content if it is off), and do not assume Foundry agent context is included
questions.question: A team enables Defender for AI Services and assumes it now covers Purview auditing, eDiscovery and insider-risk review of AI interactions, including Foundry agent conversations, with prompt text visible in every alert. Which corrections are needed?
questions.source_quote: Microsoft Defender for Cloud AI threat protection provides runtime detection of AI-specific attacks such as direct and indirect prompt injection and data exfiltration attempts, with alerts correlated in Defender XDR.

questions.explanation: Correct: at the Low threshold, content detected at low, medium and high severity is filtered, which is the strictest configuration; Medium filters medium and high only. A is wrong: High is not the strictest; it filters only high-severity content. C is wrong: the default is Medium, not Low. D is wrong: thresholds are configurable per prompt and per completion.
options: Set the threshold to High, because High is the strictest filtering configuration
Keep the default Medium, because Medium filters low, medium and high severity content
Set the threshold to Low, because Low filters content detected at low, medium and high severity, which is the strictest configuration
Accept that thresholds cannot be changed separately for prompts and completions
questions.question: A safety team wants the strictest possible content filtering on a Foundry deployment, filtering even low-severity hate content in both prompts and completions. Which threshold do they set?
questions.source_quote: Low, medium, high: Strictest filtering configuration. Content detected at severity levels low, medium, and high is filtered. Medium, high: Content detected at severity level low is not filtered, content at medium and high is filtered.

questions.explanation: Correct: a medium-severity completion is filtered at the default Medium threshold, while low-severity content is not filtered at that threshold. B is wrong: low-severity content passes at the Medium threshold. C is wrong: the filter applies to completions as well as prompts. D is wrong: the default is Medium, not High.
options: The medium-severity completion is filtered and the low-severity prompt is not, because the default Medium threshold filters medium and high severity only
Both are filtered, because the default threshold filters low severity too
Neither is filtered, because the filter only applies to prompts
The medium-severity completion passes and the low-severity prompt is filtered, because the default is High
questions.question: With the default Foundry content filter, a prompt is classified low severity for hate and the completion is classified medium severity for violence. What happens to each?
questions.source_quote: The default content filtering configuration is set to filter at the medium severity threshold for all four content harms categories for both prompts and completions. That means that content that is detected at severity level medium or high is filtered, while content detected at severity level low or safe is not filtered.

questions.explanation: Correct: protected-material text and code models are optional and on by default, and some models are required to be on for certain scenarios to retain coverage under the Customer Copyright Commitment, so turning them off can remove that coverage. A is wrong: protected-material models are on by default. B is wrong: turning them off can affect copyright-commitment coverage. D is wrong: the models are configurable on and off per scenario.
options: Protected-material models are off by default and never affect copyright coverage
Turning protected-material models off has no effect on any Microsoft commitment
Protected-material models cannot be turned off at all
Protected-material models are on by default, and some are required to be on for certain scenarios to retain coverage under the Customer Copyright Commitment
questions.question: A team wants to turn off protected-material text and code models to reduce false positives on code completions. What is the copyright risk they must check first?
questions.source_quote: Prompt shields and protected text and code models are optional and on by default. Some models are required to be on for certain scenarios to retain coverage under the Customer Copyright Commitment.

questions.explanation: Correct: the content filtering system does not apply to audio models such as Whisper, so an audio pipeline needs a different guardrail; the text filter default is Medium. A is wrong: the text filter does not cover Whisper audio. C is wrong: the filter applies to text and image models; Whisper is the exclusion. D is wrong: there is no audio-specific severity threshold in the content filter.
options: Set the audio filter threshold to High, because the text filter has a separate audio severity scale
The default Medium text filter also screens Whisper audio transcripts automatically
The content filtering system does not apply to audio models such as Whisper, so the audio pipeline needs a separate guardrail and cannot rely on the text filter
Whisper is the only model the content filter applies to
questions.question: A team builds a voice assistant on a Whisper audio model in Foundry and assumes the default content filter protects it the same way it protects text models. What is wrong?
questions.source_quote: Azure OpenAI in Microsoft Foundry Models includes default safety settings applied to all models (excluding audio API models such as Whisper).

questions.explanation: Correct: every prompt, document, retrieved chunk, tool result and memory write is treated as untrusted input, and the defence is prompt-attack detection, content filtering, sanitisation and retrieval validation, because indirect injection arrives through grounding data. B is wrong: trusting retrieved content is exactly the vulnerability. C is wrong: content filters screen prompts and completions; they do not validate retrieval permissions. D is wrong: a system prompt is not a security boundary against injected instructions in retrieved data.
options: Treat every retrieved chunk and tool result as untrusted input, and apply prompt-attack detection, content filtering and retrieval validation before it influences the model
Trust retrieved documents because they come from the companys own SharePoint
Rely on the content filter alone, because it validates retrieval permissions
Add a stronger system prompt telling the model to ignore injected instructions, because that is a sufficient boundary
questions.question: A retrieval-augmented generation app grounds answers in SharePoint documents and web pages. An attacker plants hidden instructions in a public web page the app retrieves. Which defence model is correct?
questions.source_quote: Every prompt, document, retrieved chunk, tool result, and memory write is treated as untrusted input. This group counters direct and indirect prompt injection, memory and context poisoning, poisoned retrieval content, hidden instructions in documents or webpages, and grounding-data compromise.

questions.explanation: Correct: for secure RAG, use permission-aware indexes, document-level access control or security trimming, managed identities, metadata filters and source citations so users and agents retrieve only authorised, traceable content. A is wrong: an index without trimming leaks documents the user cannot open. B is wrong: a single service identity breaks user-level access boundaries. D is wrong: citations are part of traceability, not decoration.
options: Index every document into one shared index with no access control, because the model will decide what to reveal
Use a single service identity for all retrieval, because per-user access is too slow
Use permission-aware indexes with document-level access control or security trimming, managed identities, metadata filters and source citations
Skip source citations, because they add latency and do not affect security
questions.question: A RAG app must answer questions from documents with mixed sensitivity: some users may read HR files, most may not. How must the retrieval layer be built so the model cannot surface a document the user cannot open?
questions.source_quote: For secure RAG, use permission-aware indexes, document-level access control or security trimming, managed identities, metadata filters, relevance controls, and source citations so users and agents retrieve only authorized, traceable content.

questions.explanation: Correct: Prompt Shields in APIM detects user-prompt jailbreak attempts and indirect injection in grounding data, and the llm-content-safety policy applies it at the gateway before the model. A is wrong: the gateway policy is the enforcement point; the model filter alone does not sit in front of every client. C is wrong: Prompt Shields covers both direct and indirect attacks. D is wrong: content safety at the gateway complements, not replaces, the deployment filter.
options: Rely on the deployment content filter only, because a gateway cannot inspect prompts
Enable Prompt Shields through the APIM llm-content-safety policy at the AI Gateway, so jailbreak and indirect injection attempts are detected before they reach the model
Enable only direct Prompt Shields, because indirect attacks cannot be detected at a gateway
Disable the deployment content filter once the gateway policy is on, because the two are the same control
questions.question: An AI Gateway in API Management fronts several Foundry deployments. The team wants jailbreak and indirect prompt-injection attempts blocked before they reach any model. Which gateway control does this?
questions.source_quote: Use configurable content filters for harmful-content categories and Prompt Shields to detect user-prompt attacks and hidden instructions embedded in documents, emails, webpages, or tool responses before they influence the model.

questions.explanation: Correct: the AI Gateway sits between clients and model deployments and integrates with Foundry Control Plane for advanced policy enforcement, with limits at project scope. A is wrong: the gateway is not a client library; it is a policy enforcement point. B is wrong: limits apply per project, not per model deployment globally. D is wrong: the gateway enforces token limits, content safety and authentication; it is not a billing report.
options: Place the AI Gateway between clients and model deployments, with token limits and quotas enforced at project scope
Install the gateway as a client library in each application, because there is no server-side gateway
Set one global token limit for all projects, because limits cannot be scoped per project
Use the gateway only as a billing report, because it cannot enforce limits
questions.question: A company has five Foundry projects sharing model deployments. Finance wants per-project token budgets enforced, not just reported. Where does the AI Gateway sit, and at what scope are limits enforced?
questions.source_quote: When you use AI Gateway with Foundry Control Plane to provide advanced policy enforcement for models, the gateway sits between clients and model deployments. Limits apply at the project level.

questions.explanation: Correct: enabling an AI Gateway for a project needs API Management Service Contributor or Owner on the API Management resource; a project-level contributor without that role cannot wire the gateway. A is wrong: project contributor is not enough. B is wrong: the gateway is a separate APIM resource, not automatic. C is wrong: Reader on APIM cannot configure the gateway.
options: Project Contributor is enough, because the gateway is part of the Foundry project
The gateway enables itself automatically when a model is deployed
Reader on the API Management resource is enough to configure the gateway
The person enabling the gateway needs the API Management Service Contributor role (or Owner) on the Azure API Management resource
questions.question: A project owner with Contributor on a Foundry project tries to enable AI Gateway for the project and is denied. Which role is actually required, and on what?
questions.source_quote: To enable AI Gateway for a project, you need the API Management Service Contributor role (or Owner) on the Azure API Management resource.

questions.explanation: Correct: Defender for Cloud AI threat protection detects direct and indirect prompt injection and data exfiltration attempts at runtime, with alerts correlated in Defender XDR and Sentinel. A is wrong: it is a runtime detection plan, not a content filter. B is wrong: it does not replace Purview auditing. D is wrong: it detects exfiltration attempts; it does not grant the model access to data.
options: Defender for AI Services is a content filter that replaces the Foundry content filter
Defender for AI Services gives runtime detection of direct and indirect prompt injection and data exfiltration attempts, with alerts correlated in Defender XDR
Defender for AI Services replaces Purview auditing and eDiscovery for AI interactions
Defender for AI Services grants the model access to data it could not otherwise read
questions.question: A SOC wants alerts when an AI workload is hit by a prompt-injection attack or tries to exfiltrate data, correlated with the rest of the estate. Which Defender capability is that, and what is it not?
questions.source_quote: Runtime detection of AI-specific attacks such as direct and indirect prompt injection and data exfiltration attempts, with alerts correlated in Defender XDR and Sentinel and hunting across Copilot Studio and Foundry logs.

questions.explanation: Correct: content filters screen prompts and completions for harmful content, Prompt Shields detects prompt attacks, and Defender for AI Services detects runtime attacks; none of them authorises a tool call. A is wrong: a filter cannot approve a tool invocation. B is wrong: Prompt Shields detects attacks; it does not grant business authorisation. D is wrong: the gateway enforces token and content policies, not business authorisation on tools.
options: None of them: content filters, Prompt Shields and Defender threat protection screen or detect attacks, but they do not replace business authorisation on tools
The content filter, because it approves every tool call the agent makes
Prompt Shields, because detecting an attack is the same as authorising a tool
The AI Gateway, because token limits are the same as tool authorisation
questions.question: An agent is about to call a payment tool. The team argues the Foundry content filter, Prompt Shields and Defender for AI Services together authorise the call. Which control actually authorises a tool invocation?
questions.source_quote: Microsoft Foundry guardrails and Azure AI Content Safety: safety services that inspect prompts and model responses.

questions.explanation: Correct: guardrails can be set at the deployment level and at the agent level, and they do not automatically merge; the team must confirm which guardrail is actually in force at each level. A is wrong: agent-level and deployment-level guardrails are separate settings. B is wrong: the deployment filter does not automatically cover the agent. D is wrong: disabling the deployment filter does not strengthen the agent.
options: Deployment-level and agent-level guardrails are the same setting and always merge
The deployment content filter automatically covers the agent, so no agent-level guardrail is needed
Confirm which guardrail is actually in force at agent level versus model deployment level, because they do not merge automatically
Disable the deployment filter, because the agent-level guardrail replaces it
questions.question: A team configures strict content filters on a model deployment and assumes the agent built on that deployment inherits them exactly. What must they verify, and why?
questions.source_quote: Microsoft Foundry guardrails and Azure AI Content Safety: safety services that inspect prompts and model responses. Use configurable content filters for harmful-content categories and Prompt Shields.

questions.explanation: Correct: modifying thresholds is allowed for all customers, but turning filters partially or fully off requires approval through the modified content filtering process, and managed customers only may apply for full control. A is wrong: turning filters off is not a self-service toggle. C is wrong: the approval is for turning filters off, not for raising thresholds. D is wrong: the process is a limited-access review, not an automatic entitlement.
options: Any customer can turn filters fully off in the portal with no approval
All customers can modify severity thresholds, but turning filters partially or fully off requires approval, and only managed customers may apply for full content filtering control
Raising a threshold from Medium to High requires approval, but turning filters off does not
Full content filtering control is available to every customer on request
questions.question: A customer wants to turn content filtering fully off for a deployment. What is the approval path, and what can any customer do without approval?
questions.source_quote: All customers have the ability to modify the content filters and configure the severity thresholds (low, medium, high). Approval is required for turning the content filters partially or fully off. Managed customers only may apply for full content filtering control.

questions.explanation: Correct: Foundry Control Plane enforces TPM rate limits and total token quotas for model deployments at project scope, and the gateway sits between clients and deployments. B is wrong: the limits are enforced by the control plane and gateway, not by the model itself. C is wrong: the limits are per project, not per user. D is wrong: concurrent requests can temporarily exceed limits until responses are processed, so limits are not a hard real-time cap on every concurrent burst.
options: Microsoft Foundry Control Plane enforces tokens-per-minute rate limits and total token quotas for model deployments at project scope, through the AI Gateway
The model itself enforces token limits with no gateway or control plane involved
Token limits are enforced per end user, not per project
Token limits are a hard real-time cap that can never be exceeded, even by concurrent requests
questions.question: Finance asks who actually enforces a Foundry projects token budget: the model, the application, or the platform? Which statement is correct, including the concurrency caveat?
questions.source_quote: Microsoft Foundry Control Plane enforces tokens-per-minute (TPM) rate limits and total token quotas for model deployments at the project scope. If you send many requests concurrently, token consumption can temporarily exceed the configured limits until responses are processed.

questions.explanation: Correct: the content filtering system uses an ensemble of multi-class classification models for four categories at four severity levels, plus optional binary classifiers for jailbreak risk, existing text and code in public repositories. A is wrong: there are four categories, not one. C is wrong: the binary classifiers are optional, not the only mechanism. D is wrong: the system is a classification ensemble, not a keyword list.
options: A single keyword list that blocks banned words

An ensemble of multi-class classification models for violence, hate, sexual and self-harm at safe, low, medium and high severity, plus optional binary classifiers for jailbreak risk, existing text and code in public repositories
Only a binary classifier for jailbreak risk, with no harm categories
A manual review queue with no automated classification
questions.question: A team asks how the Foundry content filtering system actually classifies content. Which description is correct?
questions.source_quote: It uses an ensemble of multi-class classification models to detect four categories of harmful content (violence, hate, sexual, and self-harm) at four severity levels respectively (safe, low, medium, and high), and optional binary classifiers for detecting jailbreak risk, existing text, and code in public repositories.

questions.explanation: Correct: a content filter must be configured on a deployment, and you must have an Azure OpenAI resource and a large language model deployment to configure content filters. B is wrong: the filter is configured per deployment, not per tenant only. C is wrong: the filter applies to the deployment model, not only to the portal UI. D is wrong: audio models are excluded, not the only covered models.
options: You must have an Azure OpenAI resource and a large language model deployment to configure content filters, and the filter is configured on that deployment
Content filters are configured once per tenant and apply to all deployments automatically with no per-deployment setting
Content filters only apply to the portal UI, not to API calls
Content filters apply only to Whisper audio models
questions.question: A team creates a Foundry project with no model deployment and tries to configure a content filter. Why does the option not exist?
questions.source_quote: You must have an Azure OpenAI resource and a large language model (LLM) deployment to configure content filters.

questions.explanation: Correct: the four categories are violence, hate, sexual and self-harm, each at safe, low, medium and high severity. A is wrong: financial advice is not a harm category. B is wrong: there are four categories, not three. D is wrong: the severity levels are safe, low, medium and high.
options: Violence, hate and sexual only, at low, medium and high severity
Violence, hate, sexual, self-harm and financial advice, at safe, low, medium and high severity
Hate, sexual and self-harm only, at safe and high severity only
Violence, hate, sexual and self-harm, each at safe, low, medium and high severity
questions.question: A policy document must list the exact harm categories and severity levels of the Foundry content filter. Which list is correct?
questions.source_quote: It uses an ensemble of multi-class classification models to detect four categories of harmful content (violence, hate, sexual, and self-harm) at four severity levels respectively (safe, low, medium, and high).

questions.explanation: Correct: Prompt Shields for direct attacks is GA and on by default, and Prompt Shields for indirect attacks is GA and off by default. A is wrong: indirect is off by default, not on. C is wrong: both are GA. D is wrong: direct is on by default.
options: Direct is off by default and indirect is on by default
Direct Prompt Shields is GA and on by default; indirect Prompt Shields is GA and off by default
Both are in preview and off by default
Direct is in preview and off, indirect is GA and on
questions.question: A compliance checklist asks for the status and default of both Prompt Shields detections. Which row is correct?
questions.source_quote: Prompt Shields for direct attacks (jailbreak): GA, On. Prompt Shields for indirect attacks: GA, Off.

questions.explanation: Correct: indirect Prompt Shields filters and annotates indirect attacks, also called cross-domain prompt injection, where third parties place malicious instructions inside documents the system can access and process. B is wrong: that describes direct jailbreak attacks. C is wrong: indirect attacks are about instructions in data, not about token limits. D is wrong: indirect Prompt Shields is a detection, not a billing control.
options: Indirect Prompt Shields filters and annotates indirect attacks, where third parties place malicious instructions inside documents the generative AI system can access and process
Indirect Prompt Shields detects user prompts that try to jailbreak the model
Indirect Prompt Shields limits token usage per minute
Indirect Prompt Shields is a billing control for token quotas
questions.question: A RAG app retrieves a document containing hidden instructions. Which Prompt Shields detection is designed for that, and what does it do?
questions.source_quote: Prompt Shields for indirect attacks: Filter / annotate Indirect Attacks, also referred to as Indirect Prompt Attacks or Cross-Domain Prompt Injection Attacks, a potential vulnerability where third parties place malicious instructions inside of documents that the generative AI system can access and process.

questions.explanation: Correct: the token-limit policy governs by token usage, and a single request can consume thousands of tokens, so call-count limits do not cap token burn. A is wrong: call-count limits do not cap tokens. C is wrong: the gateway enforces the limit before the backend is called. D is wrong: the TPM limit is per project, not per user.
options: Call-count limits cap token burn, because every call uses the same number of tokens
Token limits are only a billing report and do not block requests
Token-based rate limiting caps token consumption per minute, because one request can consume thousands of tokens and call-count limits do not cap token burn
Token limits apply per end user, so a shared deployment cannot be protected
questions.question: A single application makes 10 calls per minute, each with a 20,000-token prompt, and exhausts the deployment quota. The call-count limit never trips. Why, and which control fixes it?
questions.source_quote: Limits apply at the project level. TPM rate limit: Limits token consumption to a configured maximum per minute. When requests exceed the TPM limit, the caller receives a 429 Too Many Requests response status code.

questions.explanation: Correct: the TPM limit and the total quota are complementary dimensions: TPM is per minute and returns 429, total quota is per period (hourly, daily, weekly, monthly or yearly) and returns 403. A is wrong: the codes are not interchangeable. C is wrong: the quota period is configurable, not fixed to one day. D is wrong: TPM is per minute, not per day.
options: TPM and total quota are the same limit with the same response code
TPM is a per-minute rate limit returning 429, and total quota is a per-period limit (hourly, daily, weekly, monthly or yearly) returning 403
Total quota is always a daily limit and cannot be set to weekly or monthly
TPM is a per-day limit returning 403, and total quota is per minute returning 429
questions.question: A team configures both a TPM limit and a total token quota on a project. How do the two limits differ in window and in response code?
questions.source_quote: Token limits have two complementary enforcement dimensions: TPM rate limit: Limits token consumption to a configured maximum per minute. When requests exceed the TPM limit, the caller receives a 429 Too Many Requests response status code. Total token quota: Limits token consumption to a configured maximum per quota period (for example, hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, or yearly). When requests exceed the quota, the caller receives a 403 Forbidden response status code.

questions.explanation: Correct: the gateway sits between clients and model deployments, and Foundry Control Plane integrates with AI Gateway for advanced policy enforcement. B is wrong: the gateway is not inside the model. C is wrong: the gateway is a policy enforcement point, not a client library. D is wrong: the gateway enforces limits; it does not merely report them.
options: The AI Gateway sits between clients and model deployments, and Foundry Control Plane integrates with it for advanced policy enforcement
The AI Gateway runs inside the model and cannot be configured separately
The AI Gateway is a client library installed in each application
The AI Gateway only reports token usage and cannot enforce limits
questions.question: An architect must explain where the AI Gateway sits in the request path. Which statement is correct?
questions.source_quote: When you use AI Gateway with Foundry Control Plane to provide advanced policy enforcement for models, the gateway sits between clients and model deployments.

questions.explanation: Correct: every prompt, document, retrieved chunk, tool result and memory write is treated as untrusted input, and the defence covers direct and indirect injection, memory and context poisoning, poisoned retrieval and grounding-data compromise. A is wrong: trusted content does not exist in this model; all inputs are untrusted. B is wrong: tool results are untrusted inputs too. D is wrong: memory writes are untrusted and can poison context.
options: Only user prompts are untrusted; retrieved documents are trusted
Only documents are untrusted; tool results are trusted
Memory writes are trusted because they come from the model itself
Every prompt, document, retrieved chunk, tool result and memory write is treated as untrusted input
questions.question: A security review of an agent asks which inputs the Zero Trust AI defence model treats as untrusted. Which answer is complete?
questions.source_quote: Every prompt, document, retrieved chunk, tool result, and memory write is treated as untrusted input. This group counters direct and indirect prompt injection, memory and context poisoning, poisoned retrieval content, hidden instructions in documents or webpages, and grounding-data compromise in the retrieval layer.

questions.explanation: Correct: the defence is to detect and sanitise with prompt-attack detection, content filtering, Unicode normalisation, hidden-markup removal and restoration techniques for adversarial perturbations. A is wrong: a system prompt is not a sanitisation control. C is wrong: blocking all external content is not the documented defence; detection and sanitisation is. D is wrong: the filter alone does not sanitise hidden markup or Unicode tricks.
options: Add a stronger system prompt telling the model to ignore injected instructions
Detect and sanitise: apply prompt-attack detection, content filtering, Unicode normalization, hidden-markup removal, and restoration techniques for adversarial perturbations
Block all external content from ever reaching the model, because sanitisation is impossible
Rely on the content filter alone, because it removes hidden markup and Unicode tricks
questions.question: An attacker hides instructions in a document using Unicode tricks and hidden markup that the model still follows. Which detection and sanitisation capability addresses that?
questions.source_quote: Detect and sanitize: apply prompt-attack detection, content filtering, Unicode normalization, hidden-markup removal, and restoration techniques for adversarial perturbations.

questions.explanation: Correct: Foundry guardrails and Azure AI Content Safety inspect prompts and model responses, with configurable content filters and Prompt Shields for user-prompt attacks and hidden instructions in documents, emails, webpages or tool responses. B is wrong: the guardrails inspect both prompts and responses. C is wrong: Prompt Shields is part of the guardrail set. D is wrong: the guardrails are the safety services, not a billing control.
options: Microsoft Foundry guardrails and Azure AI Content Safety inspect prompts and model responses, using configurable content filters and Prompt Shields for user-prompt attacks and hidden instructions in documents, emails, webpages or tool responses
Foundry guardrails inspect only model responses, never prompts
Prompt Shields is not part of Foundry guardrails
Foundry guardrails are a billing control, not a safety service
questions.question: A team must name the technologies that inspect prompts and responses in a Foundry app. Which statement is correct?
questions.source_quote: Microsoft Foundry guardrails and Azure AI Content Safety: safety services that inspect prompts and model responses. Use configurable content filters for harmful-content categories and Prompt Shields to detect user-prompt attacks and hidden instructions embedded in documents, emails, webpages, or tool responses before they influence the model.

questions.explanation: Correct: Azure AI Search is the enterprise retrieval service for secure RAG, with permission-aware indexes, document-level access control, managed identities, metadata filters and source citations. A is wrong: a shared index with no access control leaks documents. C is wrong: relevance controls alone do not enforce access. D is wrong: citations are part of traceability.
options: Use a shared index with no access control, because the model filters results
Use relevance ranking only, because ranking enforces access
Use Azure AI Search with permission-aware indexes, document-level access control or security trimming, managed identities, metadata filters and source citations
Skip metadata filters, because they do not affect security
questions.question: A RAG app uses Azure AI Search for retrieval. Which search configuration keeps retrieval permission-aware and traceable?
questions.source_quote: Azure AI Search: an enterprise retrieval service for full-text, vector, semantic, hybrid, and agentic search. For secure RAG, use permission-aware indexes, document-level access control or security trimming, managed identities, metadata filters, relevance controls, and source citations.

questions.explanation: Correct: Defender for Cloud Apps discovers and risk-rates generative AI apps in use, and secure gateways inspect external content channels, reducing the chance that untrusted webpages, email or SaaS content becomes malicious grounding data. A is wrong: the control is discovery and inspection, not blocking all external content. C is wrong: Defender for Cloud Apps is a discovery control, not a model filter. D is wrong: the gateway inspects content; it does not grant the model access.
options: Block all external content from ever being retrieved

Use Defender for Cloud Apps for app discovery and session controls, and secure web or email gateways to inspect external content channels, reducing the chance untrusted content becomes malicious grounding data
Use Defender for Cloud Apps as the model content filter, because it replaces Foundry guardrails
Use the gateway to grant the model access to external content it could not otherwise read
questions.question: An agent retrieves content from public web pages and SaaS apps. Which control reduces the chance that untrusted external content becomes malicious grounding data?
questions.source_quote: Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps and secure web or email gateways: controls for discovering cloud-app use and inspecting external content channels. Use app discovery, session controls, file and URL analysis, malware detection, reputation checks, and access policies to reduce the chance that untrusted webpages, email, or SaaS content becomes malicious grounding data.

questions.explanation: Correct: adversarial test harnesses submit representative and adversarial inputs, including prompt-injection, data-exfiltration, encoding and tool-manipulation tests, and record whether defences detected, blocked or safely handled them. B is wrong: a harness tests defences; it does not prove the model is safe by itself. C is wrong: the tests include encoding and tool manipulation, not only direct prompts. D is wrong: the harness records detection and blocking, not only latency.
options: Use AI security scanners and adversarial test harnesses that submit prompt-injection, data-exfiltration, encoding and tool-manipulation tests and record whether defences detected, blocked or safely handled them
Run one benign prompt and declare the app safe if it answers correctly
Test only direct user prompts, because indirect attacks cannot be tested
Measure only response latency, because speed proves the defences work
questions.question: Before launch, a team must prove its Foundry app resists prompt injection and data exfiltration. Which testing approach is correct?
questions.source_quote: AI security scanners and adversarial test harnesses: a category of tools rather than a single product. They submit representative and adversarial inputs, including prompt-injection, data-exfiltration, encoding, and tool-manipulation tests, then record whether defenses detected, blocked, or safely handled them.

questions.explanation: Correct: the OWASP mapping is LLM01 Prompt Injection and LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses, addressed by treating prompts, retrieved content, documents, memory and tool results as untrusted, with prompt-attack detection, sanitisation, source scoring, access controls and retrieval validation. A is wrong: the mapping is LLM01 and LLM08, not LLM02 and LLM05. B is wrong: the defence is layered, not a single system prompt. D is wrong: the group covers vector and embedding weaknesses as well as prompt injection.
options: LLM02 and LLM05, addressed by a stronger system prompt
LLM01 only, addressed by content filtering alone
LLM08 only, addressed by encrypting the vector index

LLM01 Prompt Injection and LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses, addressed by treating all inputs as untrusted with prompt-attack detection, sanitisation, source scoring, access controls and retrieval validation
questions.question: A risk register must map the retrieval-hygiene control group to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM. Which mapping and defence set is correct?
questions.source_quote: OWASP Top 10 for LLM and Generative AI (2025): Maps to LLM01 Prompt Injection and LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses by treating prompts, retrieved content, documents, memory, and tool results as untrusted. Prompt-attack detection, sanitization, source scoring, access controls, and retrieval validation reduce direct and indirect injection and insecure grounding paths.

questions.explanation: Correct: with user prompt evidence disabled, Defender still analyses prompts and responses but masks the content in alerts; detection continues. A is wrong: disabling evidence does not stop detection. B is wrong: the content is masked, not deleted from analysis. D is wrong: prompt evidence is about alert content, not about whether the plan is enabled.
options: Disabling prompt evidence stops Defender from analysing prompts entirely
With user prompt evidence disabled, Defender still analyses prompts and responses but masks the content in alerts, so triage loses the suspicious prompt segments
Disabling prompt evidence deletes all prompt data from Defender permanently
Prompt evidence controls whether the Defender for AI Services plan is enabled at all
questions.question: A privacy team asks to disable user prompt evidence in Defender for AI Services. What actually changes, and what keeps working?
questions.source_quote: Runtime detection of AI-specific attacks such as direct and indirect prompt injection and data exfiltration attempts, with alerts correlated in Defender XDR and Sentinel and hunting across Copilot Studio and Foundry logs.

questions.explanation: Correct: the gateway needs a v2-tier API Management instance in the same tenant and subscription as the Foundry resource, and the enabler needs API Management Service Contributor or Owner. B is wrong: the gateway is not tenant-independent. C is wrong: a v1-tier instance does not satisfy the requirement. D is wrong: Reader cannot enable the gateway.
options: The AI Gateway needs a v2-tier API Management instance in the same tenant and subscription as the Foundry resource, and the enabler needs API Management Service Contributor or Owner on it
The AI Gateway works with any API Management tier in any tenant
A v1-tier API Management instance is sufficient for the AI Gateway
Reader on the API Management resource is enough to enable the gateway
questions.question: A team tries to enable AI Gateway with a v1-tier API Management instance in a different subscription. It fails. Which requirement is missed?
questions.source_quote: The API Management instance is in the same Microsoft Entra tenant and the same subscription as the Foundry resource. The API Management instance is created in one of the v2 tiers. You have at least the API Management Service Contributor role (or Owner) on the API Management instance.
questions.source_title: Configure AI Gateway in your Foundry resources

questions.explanation: Correct: the default is Medium for all four categories for both prompts and completions, so medium and high are filtered and low and safe are not. A is wrong: low-severity content is not filtered at Medium. B is wrong: the default is not High. D is wrong: the filter applies to both prompts and completions.
options: Low, medium and high severity content is filtered at the default
The default is High, so only high-severity content is filtered
Medium and high severity content is filtered and low and safe content is not, because the default threshold is Medium for prompts and completions
Only prompts are filtered at the default; completions are never filtered
questions.question: A prompt is classified low severity and the completion medium severity for the same category. With the default filter, which is blocked?
questions.source_quote: The default content filtering configuration is set to filter at the medium severity threshold for all four content harms categories for both prompts and completions. That means that content that is detected at severity level medium or high is filtered, while content detected at severity level low or safe is not filtered by the content filters.

questions.explanation: Correct: Prompt Shields for direct attacks is on by default and indirect is off by default, so a document attack passes the default configuration unless indirect Shields is enabled. A is wrong: direct Shields does not catch document attacks. C is wrong: the content filter screens harmful content; it does not detect hidden instructions in documents. D is wrong: indirect Shields is the missing control, not the TPM limit.
options: Direct Prompt Shields catches document attacks, so nothing is missing
Indirect Prompt Shields is off by default, so hidden instructions in documents pass unless it is enabled; the content filter alone does not detect them
The content filter detects hidden instructions in documents, so Prompt Shields is unnecessary
The TPM limit is the missing control, because it blocks document attacks
questions.question: An agent with default Foundry guardrails follows hidden instructions in a retrieved contract. The team assumed the defaults protected it. Which default is the gap?
questions.source_quote: Prompt Shields for direct attacks (jailbreak): GA, On. Prompt Shields for indirect attacks: GA, Off. Filter / annotate Indirect Attacks, also referred to as Cross-Domain Prompt Injection Attacks.

questions.explanation: Correct: Foundry Control Plane enforces TPM and total quotas at project scope, and concurrent requests can temporarily exceed limits until responses are processed, so a burst can overshoot before enforcement catches up. B is wrong: limits are enforced, not merely reported. C is wrong: limits are per project, not per user. D is wrong: the TPM limit is per minute, not per hour.
options: Foundry Control Plane enforces TPM rate limits and total quotas at project scope, but concurrent requests can temporarily exceed the configured limits until responses are processed
Token limits are only a billing report and never block requests
Token limits are enforced per end user, so a shared project cannot overshoot
The TPM limit is a per-hour limit, so a one-minute burst cannot exceed it
questions.question: A project exceeds its TPM limit during a burst of concurrent requests, even though the limit was set correctly. Why can that happen?
questions.source_quote: Microsoft Foundry Control Plane enforces tokens-per-minute (TPM) rate limits and total token quotas for model deployments at the project scope. If you send many requests concurrently, token consumption can temporarily exceed the configured limits until responses are processed.

questions.explanation: Correct: the deployment-level TPM limit caps everyone sharing the deployment, while the AI Gateway per-project limit caps one project, so the gateway limit is the fix for one project starving another. A is wrong: the deployment limit caps all projects sharing it. B is wrong: a call-count limit does not cap token burn. D is wrong: the gateway is the enforcement point, not a report.
options: Lower the deployment-level TPM limit, because that caps only the offending project
Set a call-count limit on the deployment, because that caps token burn
Remove the gateway, because it cannot enforce per-project limits
Set a per-project token limit through the AI Gateway, because a deployment-level limit caps every project sharing the deployment
questions.question: Two Foundry projects share one model deployment. One project starves the other of tokens. A developer proposes lowering the deployment-level TPM limit. Why does that miss the requirement, and what is the fix?
questions.source_quote: Limits apply at the project level. That is, each project can have its own TPM and quota settings. When you use AI Gateway with Foundry Control Plane to provide advanced policy enforcement for models, the gateway sits between clients and model deployments.

questions.explanation: Correct: Defender for AI Services is the Defender for Cloud plan for Foundry workloads, DSPM for AI is the Purview visibility capability, and Foundry guardrails screen prompts and completions; none of them is the Copilot Studio real-time protection control, which is a separate Defender capability. A is wrong: DSPM does not block tool calls. C is wrong: the content filter screens text; it does not block a tool invocation. D is wrong: Defender for AI Services is for Foundry workloads, not Copilot Studio real-time protection.
options: DSPM for AI blocks the tool call in real time

Defender for AI Services protects Foundry workloads, DSPM for AI gives data-risk visibility, and Foundry guardrails screen prompts and completions; Copilot Studio real-time protection is a separate Defender capability
The Foundry content filter blocks the tool call directly
Defender for AI Services is the Copilot Studio real-time protection control, so no other control is needed
questions.question: A Copilot Studio agent is about to exfiltrate data through a tool call. The team lists Defender for AI Services, DSPM for AI and Foundry content filters as the controls. Which statement correctly separates their jobs?
questions.source_quote: Runtime detection of AI-specific attacks such as direct and indirect prompt injection and data exfiltration attempts, with alerts correlated in Defender XDR and Sentinel and hunting across Copilot Studio and Foundry logs.
